analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every American affordable, comprehensive health insurance through federally funded state coverage plans with required employer contributions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote; it died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have sent federal matching funds to states to cover uninsured residents, first those with family incomes up to 300% of the poverty line, then everyone, with universal coverage required by 2009. Health plans would have to meet a generous benefit standard with capped premiums and cost-sharing, no preexisting-condition exclusions, and mental health parity. Employers would have to contribute at least 80% of their workers' premiums, and the bill also folded in patient-protection and medical-whistleblower protections.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 43.6 million uninsured Americans named in the bill's findings, especially lower-income families who would pay no premiums below 150% of poverty and sharply capped premiums and cost-sharing above that, plus workers whose employers would have to pay most of the premium and people with mental health or substance abuse needs who would gain full Medicare parity [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: States receive federal allotments to cover residents up to 300% of poverty, with a schedule to close the uninsured gap 50% in two years and fully in four; all states must reach universal coverage for eligible residents by 2009 [S2][S3].

Families below 150% of poverty pay no premium and cost-sharing is capped at 0.5% of income; above that, premiums and cost-sharing are capped as a share of family income, and no preexisting-condition exclusions are allowed [S3].

Employers with under 500 employees must contribute at least 80% of premiums (capped at 10% of each employee's wages), and workers can sue noncompliant employers for back contributions, liquidated damages, and attorney's fees [S3].

Medicare enrollees get full mental health and substance abuse parity, the bill incorporates the Senate-passed Bipartisan Patient Protection Act and a whistleblower protection bill, and qualified plans must spend at least 90% of premium income on actual care [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, which must fund at least 80% of employee health premiums (large employers paying above-average wages can instead cover workers directly plus an extra 1% of payroll); health insurers, which face a 90% medical-loss floor and annual competitive bidding; and taxpayers generally, since the bill's nonbinding statement that costs be offset by surpluses, health savings, or reduced tax benefits for top-bracket individuals and large corporations would not itself raise revenue [S3].

drawbacks.text: The open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') makes the federal cost unlimited on paper; the offsets in the sense-of-Congress section are nonbinding, so in practice taxpayers would bear the bill [S3].

States that fail to submit or win approval for a universal plan would be in violation and subject to lawsuits by their own residents, raising federalism and cost concerns for states that could not afford compliance [S3].
The employer mandate is a real cost on businesses, and the private right of action with mandatory attorney's fees would generate litigation over compliance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: near-universal coverage with strong consumer protections and employer premium support. The honest cost concerns are fiscal design and federalism — unlimited federal appropriations and lawsuits against states for failing to comply are poorly drawn, though the employer mandate includes wage-percentage limits that soften the burden on low-wage employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to their health subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) introduced the bill on May 11, 2004, joined by eight other House Democrats as original sponsors [S1][S3][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
On May 20 and 21, 2004, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee of each committee; the record shows no further action [S5].
The bill attracted 15 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party, in a Congress where Republicans held the House majority [S1][S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2005, with the bill never reported out of committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers were spared the employer premium mandate and the 90% medical-loss requirement, and the uninsured gained nothing; the bill's sponsors and cosponsors bore no political cost for a bill that never came up.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers; the uninsured gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill in a House controlled by a Republican majority [S4].

industries.note: Qualified private plans would gain millions of publicly funded enrollees, locking them in as the delivery channel for state universal coverage plans — but they would also face a 90% medical-loss floor, annual competitive bidding, capped cost-sharing, a ban on preexisting-condition exclusions, and public disclosure of insurer-provider financial arrangements [S3].
Employers would owe at least 80% of employee premiums (capped at 10% of wages) and face employee lawsuits with liquidated damages and attorney's fees for noncompliance [S3].

A sense-of-Congress provision calls for funding the bill partly by reducing federal tax benefits available only to individuals and corporations in the maximum tax brackets, though it would be nonbinding [S3].

industries.industry: Home care providers and health care workers
industries.note: Health plans would have to create entities serving as statutory employers of home care providers, bringing tax withholding, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation; workers would also gain notice, first-refusal rights, and whistleblower-style protections [S3].
